This is the brake. Damping only L11 head 3 to ×0.2 gives +18.6 ± 3.1 points (49 wrong→right, only 7 right→wrong). Accuracy goes from 18.6% to 37.2%, cut-offs fall from 28% to 6.6%, and answers shrink from 346 to 209 tokens.

It is much larger than the +10 from boosting head 2 ×5. That edit also damped heads 0 and 1 relative to the rest, so those two heads are useful, and the harm comes specifically from head 3. One component, a global-layer head whose content-independent attention lands on the end-of-prompt token, is holding the model back by about 19 points. That matches the task's description.

Next I want to know what exactly head 3 writes that does the damage, so that the repair can be as targeted as possible. Any of these would show the signature of a deliberately inserted component:
- an outsized dominant direction in its output block or OV circuit, compared with its siblings;
- a rank-1 spike, i.e. a natural head plus one added write direction;
- an output that mostly re-writes a particular input direction, such as the math-mode direction.

So I compare the singular spectra of the four L11 output blocks and OV circuits. I also check how head 3's dominant read and write directions relate to the massive dimensions, to D1 (the math-mode direction at L10), and to the residual mean at the end of the prompt. I also record the result in the notes and back the edit up.

The spike alone does not single head 3 out. Rank-1 spikes in head output blocks are common in this model: L21h2 (5.10), L17h1 (4.97) and several late-layer sink heads exceed head 3's S0/S1 of 2.44 (median 1.6). What does stand out is the size of head 3's actual output. For the mean end-of-prompt state it writes a vector of norm 10.8, about twice its siblings' (5.9, 3.6, 5.0), and 27% of that runs along its spike direction u.

The spike direction is unusually concentrated: 50 of the 1,152 residual dimensions carry 85% of it. It is not the massive dimensions (3%) and not the math-mode direction.

That suggests a specific way head 3 could act as a brake, which also explains why boosting head 2 helped. L11's post-attention RMSNorm divides the sum of the four heads' outputs by its RMS. A head writing a large, fixed vector inflates that RMS and so shrinks everything the other heads retrieve. If that vector lands mainly in dimensions where the post-norm scale (1+w) is small, it carries little information forward and acts purely as a "volume knob" on L11's useful attention.

I check this from the weights:
- the post-norm scales on the spike's 50 dominant dimensions and on head 3's mean-state output, against the layer median;
- head 3's share of the summed L11 attention output for the mean end-of-prompt state;
- the logit-lens effect of head 3's post-norm write on a few task-relevant tokens, compared with head 2's.

A "drowning" brake would show large raw energy in low-scale dimensions. A semantic brake would show strong effects on tokens such as EOS, newline or "####".

Run 149 supports a specific mechanism. Head 3's dominant (spike) output direction puts most of its raw energy in dimensions that L11's post-attention norm almost discards: median gain |1+w| = 0.67 there, against 15.4 for the layer. So the spike mainly inflates the RMS that divides all four heads' outputs. At the mean end-of-prompt state, head 3 supplies 57% of L11's summed raw attention output, and after the norm it writes 3–6× more than its siblings. Through the logit lens, that write strongly suppresses `<end_of_turn>` (z = −3.1) and promotes digits and newlines. That fits the run-on, cut-off answers that the S3 edit largely removed (cut-offs 28% → 6.6%).

Two mechanisms remain possible:
- the rank-1 spike dilutes the useful heads through the norm;
- head 3's main write itself does the harm.

To separate them, I build the most targeted repair, R1a. It projects only the spike's output direction u0 out of head 3's output columns: B → (I − u0u0ᵀ)B, a single direction in 256 columns, with heads 0–2 untouched. I will test it next on the same slice where S3 gave +18.6 (DEV[1024:1250]).
- If R1a recovers most of that gain, the spike is the brake and R1a is the precise undo.
- If it does little, the harm lies in head 3's main write, and whole-head damping (with a dose scan) is the right edit.

I also break down where S3's gain came from (cut-off vs finished-wrong answers), check that the S3 backup exists, and log the plan before the pass.
